intro: In English, most nouns take -s in the plural, and you pronounce this -s. But there are spelling rules, irregular plurals (men, children, people) and some nouns with no plural at all (information, advice).
objectifs: Make regular plurals and use the spelling rules (-es, -ies, -ves).
Know the most common irregular plurals.
Recognise nouns that are always plural (jeans, trousers) and uncountable nouns with no plural (information, advice, furniture).

texte: The general rule is to add -s: a book → two books. Some endings need a different spelling, often to make the word easier to say. These rules are the same as the -s of the present simple (lesson 6).
Adjectives never take -s in English: big houses, red cars (never “bigs houses”).

lignes: car → cars, day → days, apple → apples
bus → buses, glass → glasses, dish → dishes, watch → watches, box → boxes
city → cities, baby → babies, country → countries
boy → boys, key → keys, holiday → holidays
potato → potatoes, tomato → tomatoes, hero → heroes
photo → photos, piano → pianos, radio → radios, video → videos

exemples: I've got two brothers and three sisters.
There are many beautiful cities in Belgium.

texte: About twelve common nouns ending in -f or -fe change to -ves: knife → knives, wife → wives, life → lives, leaf → leaves, half → halves, shelf → shelves, wolf → wolves, thief → thieves.
Others just add -s: roof → roofs, chief → chiefs, belief → beliefs, chef → chefs, cliff → cliffs. If you are not sure, check in the dictionary.
exemples: Put the knives in the drawer.
The leaves are yellow in October.

texte: Some very common nouns have an irregular plural. Learn them by heart: you use them every day.
“People” is the normal plural of “person”: two people, ten people. “Persons” is only for official texts.
exemples: There are twenty people in the room.
The women in my family are very tall.

texte: Some things made of two parts are always plural in English, with a plural verb: trousers, jeans, shorts, glasses (for your eyes), scissors, pyjamas. To count them, say “a pair of”: a pair of jeans, two pairs of glasses. “Clothes” has no singular.
“People” and “police” are always plural: The police are here. People are nice.

On the other hand, some uncountable nouns have no plural in English: information, advice, news (singular verb), furniture, luggage, homework, hair. Don't say “an information” or “informations”. You will study them in lesson 59.

lignes: I've got a lot of luggages.
I've got a lot of luggage.

texte: After a number bigger than one, and after “these, those, many, a few, both”, a countable noun is plural: two cats, these shoes, many people.
A noun used like an adjective before another noun stays singular: a ten-euro note, a three-day trip, a shoe shop.
exemples: We need six eggs and two kilos of tomatoes.

formule: noun + s · -s / -sh / -ch / -x + es · consonant + y → ies · -f(e) → ves (often) · irregular: men, women, children, people, feet, teeth
prononciation: The -s sounds like /s/ after p, t, k, f: cats /kæts/, books, cups.
It sounds like /z/ after a vowel or a voiced sound: dogs /dɒɡz/, days, cars, knives /naɪvz/.
-es / -s sounds like /ɪz/ (one more syllable) after s, z, sh, ch, j, x sounds: buses /ˈbʌsɪz/, watches, boxes, pages /ˈpeɪdʒɪz/.
“woman” /ˈwʊmən/ and “women” /ˈwɪmɪn/: the first syllable changes when you speak, not the second.
“houses” is /ˈhaʊzɪz/: the s of “house” becomes /z/ in the plural.
erreurs: The normal plural of person is people.
A noun before another noun stays singular.

dialogue.contexte: Before a picnic in the Parc de la Tête d'Or in Lyon, two flatmates write a shopping list.
lignes: How many people are coming to the picnic?
Twelve: eight adults and four children.
OK. So we need bread, cheese, tomatoes and some potatoes for a salad.
And knives, forks and glasses. Have we got enough?
We've got six knives. Let's buy plastic ones.
No, it's bad for the planet. My parents have got a lot of knives. I can ask them.
Good idea. Oh, and the news says it's sunny tomorrow.
Great! I need my sunglasses and my new shorts.

mots: I brush my teeth twice a day.
one of the white things in your mouth (plural: teeth)
the part of your body at the end of your leg (plural: feet)
Can I have a knife, please?
a vegetable that grows under the ground
two lenses in a frame to help you see (always plural)

exercices.consigne: Write the sentence in the plural.
Each sentence has one mistake. Correct it.
items: There are ten persons on the bus.
There are ten people on the bus.

exercices.consigne: Complete the sentence with the plural of the word in brackets.
items: My ___ hurt. I walk a lot. (foot)
Where are my ___? I can't see! (glasses)
There are three ___ in this town. (library)

exercices.consigne: Describe what is in your kitchen or your bag in four sentences. Use at least one irregular or -ves plural and one noun that is always plural.
items: In my bag there are two pens, three keys and my glasses. In my kitchen there are four knives and six glasses. I've got a lot of boxes on the shelves. My children's photos are on the fridge.

a_retenir: Noun + s; + es after s, sh, ch, x; consonant + y → ies; often -f(e) → ves.
Irregular: men, women, children, people, feet, teeth, mice; no change: sheep, fish.
Always plural: trousers, jeans, glasses, scissors, clothes, people, police.
No plural: information, advice, news (singular verb), furniture, luggage, homework.
